newsitem.title: UK: Pre-emptive rate rise may boost British gilts.
newsitem.headline: Pre-emptive rate rise may boost British gilts.

text.p: British gilts may power ahead of other European debt markets, viewing a quarter point interest rate rise on Friday as a necessary pre-emptive strike against building inflation, analysts said.
The market's positive outlook will also be helped by gilts' position as a safe haven from the turmoil facing continental Europe over the single currency project.
"I think this will be taken as a preventative move and they won't have to raise rates for quite a while," said Gianpaolo Mosconi, bond analyst Sanwa International in London.
"On that basis gilts offer value against other European markets and I would expect the spread over Bunds to move towards 135 to 130 over the next couple of weeks," he added.

Meeting for the first time since Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown granted the Bank of England independence to set interest rates, the monetary policy committee raised British official rates to 6.50 percent from 6.25 percent previously.

"This is not necessarily a negative thing for gilts," said Andrew Snowball, UK Treasury economist at Co-operative Bank in London. "The monetary policy committee has shown that it is prepared to use the new powers it has been given and that can only be good for its credibility."
He likened it to the previous increase in rates in May, which came with the announcement of the Bank's independence, saying the outlook was little changed on the news.

"The move was priced fully into the cash market and short sterling futures. The short sterling futures implicitly assume base rates will rise by another quarter of a percent between now and the end of the year," Snowball said, adding that the Bank of England's statement on Friday backed that up.
The statement said; "on present evidence, there is still likely to be a need for some further moderate tightening of policy in the months ahead."
September short sterling futures were at 93.14, down 0.03 on the day, while the December contract was at 92.99, down two basis points.
Mosconi said there was one cloud on the horizon for gilts -- the glut of money hitting the economy as a rash of building societies convert to banks this summer.
Sanwa forecasts the conversions will result in around a 30 billion pound ($48.8 billion) infusion into the economy.
"It means that retail sales are likely to stay strong over the next couple of months but on balance we don't expect the BOE to continue raising rates (dramatically)," he said.
He said the maximum rise would be around the 50 basis point increase forward markets were pricing in.
Sonja Gibbs, senior bond strategist at Nomura International in London, said the market would find reassurance in the Bank of England demonstrating it was not going to be behind the yield curve.
"Moreover we look for the budget to be market friendly as well -- fiscal tightening, responsible, maybe even having a few innovative features," she said.
The Chancellor will unveil the budget on July 2. Analysts said uncertainty over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would also boost gilts, narrowing the 10-year gilt/Bund yield spread.
The spread is currently at 140 basis points compared with 185 at the beginning of January.
"Over the next few months I can see the spread closing in to under 100 basis points," said Snowball.
"Gilts are good on a convergence trade not because we are going into a single currency, but because we are not." ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
